newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - G7 seen as only impediment to dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - G7 seen as only impediment to dollar rise.

text.p: A chorus of anti-dollar remarks from Group of Seven (G7) nations at a meeting next month may be the only factor now which could shoot down the dollar, but analysts said on Wednesday that such a scenario was unlikely.

Rosy economic factors have pushed the dollar to its highest level against the yen in nearly four years and a 31-month peak on the mark. And it would take a very radical shift in fundamentals to change the trend substantially, they said.

"There's no evidence either at this point that there's huge resistance from policymakers in Europe, the U.S. or Japan against the (dollar's) move," said Chase Investment Bank chief economist Robin Marshall, although he said it was time for a dollar adjustment after its recent breathtaking rally.
By midday on Wednesday the dollar was at 1.6505 marks and 122.15 yen, down from its high of 1.6555 marks and 122.78 yen, but up from 1.6468 and 121.15 at the European close on Tuesday.
One of the key events next week will be a policy-making meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on February 4 and 5.

This is not likely to disturb currencies much because even if the Federal Reserve does not raise rates next week, which many analysts say is the likely decision, the market firmly believes it will do so in the near future.

"The dollar is being boosted by expectations that there will be an increase in U.S. rates, not necessarily at the next FOMC but almost certainly at the one after that," said Julian Fisher, international economist at Daiwa Europe.

Of far more interest was the planned meeting in Berlin on February 8 of finance ministers and central bank governors from the G7 industrialised nations -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada.
Analysts saw very little chance of anything definitive emerging on currencies -- mainly because the U.S., Germany and Japan are content with the dollar's direction.

"It would take quite strong words from the G7 to have a dampening effect on the dollar... But everyone's enjoying the dollar's strength at the moment although no-one wants to endorse this," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns.

In Germany's case, the domestic economy is so subdued that any inflationary threat caused by the mark's weakness would not be much of a problem. Chase's Marshall said that for Germany's commercial purposes, the mark's performance against other European currencies was more important.
As far as Japan is concerned, a weak yen is helping its exporting industry -- a mainstay of its economy -- and hence the Tokyo stock market.

Although there has been plentiful rhetoric from Japanese authorities about how an excessively weak yen would be unfavourable, analysts said this was their way of pacing the dollar's rally without actually intervening.
"The (Japanese) Ministry of Finance and Bank of Japan basically want to ensure that any dollar rally is managed," Fisher said.

Analysts were mixed about how far the dollar's rise might go without a major turnaround. Some cited 125 yen and 1.67 marks as a near-term ceiling. Many said the dollar would undergo a slight correction ahead of the G7 meeting.
"The momentum isn't going to change quickly. But technically the dollar's overbought, and there must be some incentive to take profits ahead of the G7 meeting," Marshall said.
Fisher expected the yen to strengthen temporarily before the end of March, as Japanese companies would be repatriating their funds ahead of the March 31 end of the business year.
